common_name: ColorBlaze Golden Dreams Coleus (Bright Chartreuse-Gold Sun-Tolerant Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; ColorBlaze Golden Dreams is a Proven Winners sun-tolerant coleus selection with brilliant chartreuse-gold foliage that glows in mixed containers and holds its bright color better in more direct sun than shade-bred coleus.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Golden Dreams, part of the Proven Winners ColorBlaze series, produces vigorous, well-branched mounds of solid chartreuse-to-gold foliage that brightens with more sun exposure while remaining scorch-resistant compared to older gold cultivars, making it a reliable 'thriller' or filler for sunny to lightly shaded combination containers and borders. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy directed into foliage production, and pinch growing tips periodically through the season to encourage a dense, mounded habit rather than leggy growth.
sources: Proven Winners — ColorBlaze Golden Dreams coleus cultivar notes
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
North Carolina State Extension — Sun-Tolerant Coleus Cultivars

common_name: ColorBlaze Marooned Coleus (Deep Maroon-Black Sun-Tolerant Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Marooned is a Proven Winners ColorBlaze coleus with dense, nearly solid deep maroon-black foliage that provides a dramatic dark-foliage anchor for sunny to lightly shaded combination plantings.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Marooned, part of the Proven Winners ColorBlaze series, forms compact, well-branched mounds of deep maroon-black leaves that read almost solid black from a distance, giving it strong impact as a dark-foliage contrast plant against brighter chartreuse or silver companions. Its improved sun tolerance compared to older dark coleus cultivars lets it hold color and habit in considerably more light. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a full, bushy shape.
sources: Proven Winners — ColorBlaze Marooned coleus cultivar notes

common_name: Sea Urchin Coleus (Spiky Deeply Lobed Burgundy-Red Under the Sea Coleus)
scientific_name: Coleus scutellarioides 'Under the Sea Sea Urchin'

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Sea Urchin, part of the Under the Sea series, bears narrow, deeply incised burgundy-red leaves that radiate outward like the spines of its namesake, an unusually fine, spiky texture among coleus cultivars.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix. Sea Urchin, part of the distinctively fine-textured Under the Sea coleus series, produces narrow, deeply lobed and pointed burgundy-red leaves that project outward in a starburst pattern reminiscent of a sea urchin's spines, an eye-catching departure from the broad, flat leaves of typical coleus. Its low, spreading, spiky mound works well planted at the front of borders or trailing over container edges, where its fine texture contrasts nicely with broader-leaved neighbors like hosta and caladium. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy in foliage, and pinch tips periodically to maintain a dense habit.
sources: Ball Horticultural Company — Under the Sea coleus series notes
North Carolina State Extension — Coleus Cultivar Trials

common_name: Freckles Coleus (Heirloom Green Coleus Speckled with Red-Magenta Spots)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Freckles is an heirloom-type shade coleus with bright green leaves heavily flecked and spotted in red-magenta, a speckled pattern distinct from the solid or veined patterns of most modern cultivars.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Freckles is a classic-style coleus bearing bright green leaves densely speckled and flecked with small red-magenta spots, a scattered, freckled pattern that reads as a soft textural blush of color rather than the bold blocks or veining of many newer cultivars. It performs best out of hot direct sun, which can scorch the thinner heirloom-type foliage, making it well suited to shaded borders, woodland-edge containers, and mixed shade combinations. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically through the season to encourage a full, bushy habit.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
North Carolina State Extension — Heirloom Coleus Cultivars

common_name: Trailing Queen Coleus (Classic Heirloom Cascading Purple-Black Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Trailing Queen is a long-grown heirloom coleus cultivar with small, deep purple-black leaves edged in green on vigorously trailing stems, traditionally used to cascade from hanging baskets and window boxes.

directions: Plant in partial to full shade in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Trailing Queen is one of the oldest and most enduring trailing coleus cultivars, bearing small, deep purple-black leaves with a narrow green edge on long, vigorously cascading stems that have made it a longtime favorite for hanging baskets, window boxes, and the edges of raised beds. Unlike the compact, upright habit of most modern bedding coleus, its stems can trail two feet or more in a single season with regular pinching to encourage fullness. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to keep the plant's energy in foliage, and pinch stem tips periodically, especially early in the season, to build a dense, well-branched cascade rather than a few long, sparse runners.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Heirloom Coleus Cultivars
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant

common_name: Inky Fingers Coleus (Narrow-Lobed Deep Purple-Black Finger-Leaf Coleus)

planting.note: Plant after all frost danger has passed; Inky Fingers bears narrow, deeply lobed, finger-like leaves in near-black deep purple, a fine-textured dark coleus selection distinct from broader-leaved dark cultivars like Black Dragon.

directions: Plant in partial shade to nearly full sun in moist, well-drained, fertile soil or container mix; Inky Fingers produces narrow, deeply lobed leaves divided into finger-like segments in a deep, near-black purple, giving the plant a fine, almost lacy texture that sets it apart from broader-leaved dark coleus cultivars such as Black Dragon. Its compact, well-branched mound holds its dark color well with some direct sun exposure, and its unusual leaf shape makes it a good textural accent against brighter chartreuse or silver-leaved companions in mixed containers. Pinch off flower spikes as they appear to redirect energy into foliage, and pinch growing tips periodically to maintain a dense, bushy habit.
sources: North Carolina State Extension — Coleus Cultivar Trials
University of Florida IFAS Extension — Coleus as Annual Foliage Plant
